claims.text: Creep resistance of the FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy protective coating is governed by formation of a stable surface oxide layer.
The surface oxide layer acts as a barrier to dislocation movement.
The surface oxide layer inhibits grain-boundary sliding.
The initial material is a polished and cleaned FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy coating.
The proposed intervention is continuous loading at elevated temperature.
The proposed operating stress range is 100-500 MPa.
The proposed operating temperature range is 500-800 °C.
Stable oxide-layer formation reduces dislocation movement and grain-boundary sliding.
The oxide-bearing material will have a lower steady-state creep rate than the stated baseline.
The oxide-bearing material will have a longer time to failure than the stated baseline.
Outside an unspecified temperature and stress boundary, the oxide layer becomes unstable or the alloy undergoes significant microstructural change.
The proposed controlled comparison is between coated and uncoated FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy samples under identical loading conditions.
Failure to observe a significant creep-resistance improvement in the coated sample would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The terminology conflates the FCC/BCC HEA protective coating with the hypothesized surface oxide coating. The initial material is already called an HEA coating, whereas the baseline and experiment use 'uncoated' or 'bare' without clarifying whether this means absence of the HEA coating or selective absence of the oxide layer. Consequently, the comparison does not clearly isolate oxide formation.
